text: Yes, training legs can affect upper body recovery — but adequate nutrition significantly reduces that interference. Here's why: The interference effect is real Research shows that combining high intensity leg training with upper body resistance exercise can acutely attenuate muscle protein synthesis signals in the upper body muscles immediately after training. However this acute attenuation disappears during the recovery period — meaning the final outcome for upper body muscle growth is largely unaffected.

text: You can isolate your biceps by propping your arm on a raised bench. If you have a good reason for not doing that, you could do all your regular sets without the bench, and only temporarily rest the arm on a readied bench at the very end, and only do the very last reps this way. If you don't mind using the bench then just use it for all reps. By supporting the upper arm at an angle you get resistance right to the bitter end of the movement (at the maximum stretch), where it counts most.

text: You are weighting yourself in grams accuracy, but you are not weighting your food! To see how much you are actually eating, you need to put every single food item you eat on a scale and convert the weight into kcal/kJ. Then, after a month or two, you'll know how many calories your regular food items have and you don't need the scale and the conversion tables anymore. I dropped from 85 kg to 75 kg (185 cm) five years ago by just calorie counting and weighting food. Now I'm at a stable 79 kg without counting and weighting.
